articles.title_orig: Benjamin Satterley, globetrotting wrestler known as PAC, dies at 40
articles.title_zh: Benjamin Satterley, globetrotting wrestler known as PAC, dies at 40
articles.content_orig:
Benjamin Satterley, the hard-hitting and high-flying professional wrestler known to fans worldwide simply as Pac, has died, All Elite Wrestling announced Sunday night. He was 40.
News of his death came the day after he’d wrestled during AEW’s “All Out” pay-per-view Saturday night at the NOW Arena in Hoffman Estates, Illinois, outside Chicago. A cause of death was not immediately provided.
“A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability,” AEW said.
Satterley first made a name for himself on the British independent scene before he embarked on a globetrotting career in which he performed in some of the biggest promotions on the planet, including AEW, World Wrestling Entertainment (where he went by Adrian Neville), New Japan Pro-Wrestling and Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre.
His high-flying offense, made all the more impressive by the brawny physique on his stocky frame, earned him the nickname “The Man That Gravity Forgot.”
Satterley debuted on All Elite Wrestling in 2019, following his stint in WWE, where he’d eventually earn the monicker “The Bastard.”
At AEW, he won the All-Atlantic Championship in 2022 and became one of the company’s more prominent wrestlers as part of the Death Riders faction, with whom he’d earn the AEW World Trios Championship alongside fellow members Claudio Castagnoli and Wheeler Yuta in 2025. It followed another Trios title in 2022 alongside Penta El Zero Miedo and Rey Fénix as part of the “Death Triangle.”
Between the ropes, few wrestlers could combine speed, agility, technique and raw power quite like Satterley.
He could twist and wind his body off the top turnbuckle with his signature “Black Arrow” maneuver, or he could use his “Brutalizer” to tie up an opponent’s arms and neck on the canvas.
On the microphone, his promos conveyed no-nonsense intensity that relayed an ultimately simple message to opponents: I’m here to hurt you.
“My name is ‘The Bastard,’” Satterley said in one AEW promo. “The people named me that because I am a bastard. But on top of that — in addition to — I just so happen to be an excellent, exceptional, world-class professional wrestler.”
Tributes to Satterley quickly followed news of his death.
“The greatest export from our country,” fellow Englishman and AEW World Champion Will Ospreay said on X . “Also the greatest human being.”
“I am in shock. This is heartbreaking,” AEW wrestler Evil Uno said . “We have lost another great person, a great soul, a true professional.”
Ace Austin, whom Satterley defeated on a special episode of AEW’s “Collision” program Wednesday, summed up what many were feeling Sunday: “I don’t understand man.”
Rudy Chinchilla is a breaking news editor for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: China posts weakest industrial profit growth this year, expanding 4.2% in August
articles.title_zh: China posts weakest industrial profit growth this year, expanding 4.2% in August
articles.content_orig:
China's industrial profits grew at their weakest pace this year, expanding just 4.2% in August from a year earlier, official data released Monday showed, as manufacturers grapple with persistent weakness in consumer demand and a sustained rise in energy costs.
The muted growth in August marked the fourth straight month of deceleration, after the 24.7% expansion in April , and the weakest performance since November 2025 when profits posted a double-digit decline.
For the first eight months of this year, profits at large industrial firms climbed 15.7%, losing momentum from a 17.6% rise in the January-July period .
The slowdown comes after industrial earnings staged a notable reversal earlier this year, swinging from a barely-positive 0.6% gain for all of 2025 — the first increase after three straight years of declines — to double-digit growth. That expansion has been led by the artificial-intelligence-fueled boom in chips and computing equipment and has coincided with the end of nearly three years of factory-gate deflation.
The earnings report also points to an increasingly bifurcated economy, with strong earnings growth in high-tech sectors, such as AI and robotics, whereas consumer-related industries like clothing, autos and furniture showed declining profits.
Yu Weining, chief statistician at NBS, attributed the deceleration in August to a high base effect from last year , when profits reversed months of declines to surge 20.4% year on year , amid Beijing's efforts to curb price wars in several industrial sectors. In the statement on Monday, Yu repeated policymakers' pledges to bolster domestic demand and "optimize" supplies.
Profits in the computer, communication and electronic equipment manufacturing industry more than doubled for the January-to-August period, rising 110% from a year earlier. The automobile manufacturing industry saw profits drop by 16% during the same period as the sector sees cut-throat competition.
Growth in the world's second-largest economy softened to its slowest in more than three years in the second quarter, as a multiyear property downturn continued to depress consumer demand and investment in real estate and infrastructure.
The official purchasing managers' index indicated that manufacturing activity contracted for two consecutive months in July and August. Retail sales slowed further , and the urban investment slump deepened in August, while industrial output rebounded on the back of exports.
Economists expect Beijing to lean harder on stimulus to stabilize corporate profitability, as consolidation accelerates in sectors already facing sluggish demand, fierce competition and cutthroat price wars.
Allan von Mehren, China economist at Danske Bank, said authorities will likely step up policy implementation in the second half of this year to shore up the economy, accelerating deployment of investment in strategic sectors, such as water, power grid, data centers, networks, urban pipelines and logistics networks.

articles.title_orig: How Lamar Jackson, Tyler Loop led Ravens to win over Cowboys in just 7 seconds
articles.title_zh: How Lamar Jackson, Tyler Loop led Ravens to win over Cowboys in just 7 seconds
articles.content_orig:
The Cowboys cost themselves a win with an odd set of decisions late in their 34-31 loss to the Ravens in Brazil.
Dallas and Baltimore were tied at 31 in a game that appeared to need overtime to decide a winner, but instead, the Ravens were the beneficiaries of some bad decision-making and came away victorious in Rio.
Down to just seven seconds left, Brandon Aubrey kicked the ball off, but instead of getting it in play to force the Ravens to run more time off the clock, he kicked it out of the end zone, allowing Baltimore a touchback.
Because of the NFL’s touchback rule, the ball was placed at Baltimore’s 35-yard line and the Ravens would get one more chance to make something happen with one timeout remaining. Lamar Jackson fired a dart to Zay Flowers in the Cowboys’ end of the field, and Baltimore managed to use their last timeout with one second on the clock.
WILD: WHAT WAS THE #COWBOYS DEFENSE DOING ON THIS PLAY 💀 There was less than 10 seconds left and it was a tie game, about to go to overtime. Zay Flowers was WIDE OPEN over the middle to put them in FG range. HISTORICALLY BAD 😬😬 pic.twitter.com/NVwxZfYEBj
Tyler Loop hit a 56-yard field goal for the win and the Cowboys were forced to head back to the United States after a heartbreaking defeat.
“Everybody nowadays with all the game management people throughout the league, you’re aware of the time constraints on these situations and what you’re able to do. The touchback rule is huge,” Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. “The 35-yard line, so we felt the same way with their kicker. When they get the ball at the 35, they’re 15 yards from being in field goal range. We felt like one play that could take six seconds, kind of know the time that route takes and the yards that we needed. Great execution by our guys and came through.”
That wasn’t the only error by the Cowboys late in the game, with quarterback Dak Prescott overthrowing George Pickens in the end zone with 14 seconds left in the game and Dallas down 31-28.
Aubrey kicked the field goal to tie the game.
“He called a quick out. I probably overcoached Dak on that one,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said.
The Cowboys are now 1-2 on the season.

articles.title_orig: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
articles.title_zh: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
articles.content_orig:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island
Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.
David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”
The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn , after a record multi-billion dollar deal was unveiled in December last year.
Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned . At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.
Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.
Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.
After Purdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times that the US had no plans to sell arms to China , while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
Before the interview, Taiwanese deputy foreign minister Chen Ming-chi spoke of the severe military threat China posed.
“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.
Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.
Perdue himself told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.

articles.title_zh: NFL Week 3 grades for all 32 teams: Ravens get 'B+' for wild Rio win, Raiders earn 'A-' for beating Saints
articles.content_orig:
The Baltimore Ravens pulled off one of the more dramatic wins of the season Sunday afternoon in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, beating the Dallas Cowboys 34-31 on a game-winning 56-yard field goal from Tyler Loop as time expired.
Dallas jumped out to a 10-0 lead, but Baltimore answered with 17 straight points and led 24-13 in the third quarter. Dak Prescott and the Cowboys fought back to go up 28-24 on a nine-yard touchdown from KaVontae Turpin. Lamar Jackson then answered with a two-yard touchdown pass to rookie Matt Hibner, putting the Ravens back on top before Dallas tied it late, setting up Loop's game-winner.
Stars on both sides showed out and gave Brazil a show, but Derrick Henry made history in the wild Ravens win. Henry ran for 89 yards and two touchdowns, both in the first half. In doing so, he passed Hall of Famer Marcus Allen for third-most career rushing touchdowns (135), including the playoffs, and now sits behind only Emmitt Smith (183) and LaDainian Tomlinson (151). Henry also moved past Eric Dickerson into ninth on the NFL 's career rushing list.
More news : Giants Targeting These 6 QBs to Replace Jaxson Dart: Report
Henry is in his 11th NFL season at 32 years old, and given his physical, downhill rushing style at over 250 pounds, you'd expect a player like that to start slowing down at this stage of his career. That hasn't happened yet. Through three weeks, the five-time Pro Bowler is still playing like one of the best running backs in football.
He already has 212 rushing yards and four rushing touchdowns this season, is averaging 5.3 yards per carry, and is in line for his fifth straight 1,000-yard season and the eighth of his career.

Emmitt Smith still holds the all-time record with 11 1,000-yard seasons. At 32, Henry still has time to catch that record, too.
Henry's next chance to build on this performance comes in Week 4, when the Ravens host the winless Titans back in Baltimore.

Former FBI investigator Bill Daly discusses the investigation into an alleged terror plot after five suspects were arrested near an airbase in southwest England on ‘Fox Report.’
Five men arrested near a key U.S. bomber base in the U.K. on Sunday may have planned a "complex," coordinated attack with potentially far-reaching security implications for American military installations globally, a former U.S. intelligence official warned.
As counterterrorism police investigated after officers detained the suspects near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, a former Pentagon official also said President Donald Trump will ultimately be the one to decide the consequences if indeed the "trail leads to Tehran."
The men were initially held on suspicion of offenses under Britain’s Explosives Act before being arrested on terrorism charges in connection with the airfield, a key U.S. Air Force hub and the primary European base for American strategic bombers.
On Sunday, Trump said U.S. authorities had been monitoring the suspects prior to their capture.

"We had them under investigation," Trump told reporters in Chicago. "They were looking to do big damage to our fort."
"It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know. We worked with a lot of them. We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," Trump added.
According to Sky News , counterterrorism police were investigating whether Iran is linked to the suspected bomb plot.
Former Trump White House official Morgan Murphy told Fox News Digital that British authorities are leading the investigation alongside U.S. law enforcement and intelligence.
"Every phone, bank record and rental receipt will be run through British and American intelligence, and if the trail leads to Tehran, it will be found," Murphy clarified.
"But as American airmen and bombers seem to have been the target, Air Force investigators on the base, the FBI in London, and American intelligence will likely all work the case."
"If conclusive evidence proves Iran is behind an attempted attack on U.S. forces, the American President will ultimately decide how Tehran pays," Murphy added.

A US Air Force Boeing B-52 Stratofortress bomber jet lands on the runway, beyond a USAF Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber jet, at RAF Fairford in southwest England on March 9, 2026. (Henry NICHOLLS / AFP via Getty Images)
Former Defense Intelligence Agency official Andrew Badger told Fox News Digital the number of suspects and vehicles involved raised the possibility of a sophisticated operation.
"We are going to see elevated security protocols across Europe , across the U.K., and across the entire world for any U.S. installation," he said.
"This is a very significant threat, and again, seeing that we had five individuals involved and three different reported vans at the scene, this could have been a very complex, highly orchestrated operation," Badger added.
"This isn't just some type of amateur lone wolf operation," he said, noting Fairford’s strategic importance to the U.S. military. "Fairford is also where the U.S. houses its strategic bombers for Europe as well as the rest of the world."
He said a potential attack posed broader risks beyond the airfield itself which he said "could have had significant security implications. It could have damaged the nearby area."
HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY
RAF Fairford is in the spotlight after five men were arrested near the key U.S. bomber base in the U.K. on Sunday. (Reuters)
"They could have tried to use a VBIED or a vehicle-borne explosive device where the first van could have gone off at the front gate, and then the other vans would have gone in and tried to go for the strategic bombers," Badger said.
British authorities have not publicly identified who they believe was behind the suspected plot or announced a motive, but RAF Fairford had taken on greater strategic importance during the war with Iran.
The U.K. government previously authorized U.S. forces to use the Royal Air Force bases Fairford and Diego Garcia for limited defensive operations, including destroying Iranian missiles and launchers at their source.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later warned that any base used to attack Iranian territory would be considered a legitimate target.
"Any base used to launch attacks on Iranian territory is a legitimate target for our forces," the IRGC said, according to reports .
"Tehran warned London in July to keep American bombers off Fairford, and if this plot traces back to Iran, the answer must be more bombers, not fewer," Morgan said.
IRAN EXPERT BRANDS ISLAMIC CENTER OF ENGLAND IRAN'S 'UK OFFICE,' URGES IMMEDIATE CLOSURE
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Chief Justice of Iran Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and an IRGC commander general Mohsen Rezaee attend a ceremony in Tehran, Iran, on July 3, 2026. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
A local councilor told Reuters there had been a recent security alert at Fairford and surveillance had been stepped up.
"So there was a specific threat about six weeks ago from the Iranians on this base. At the time, there was increased surveillance around the area," he told the outlet .
Badger, however, cautioned against assuming Iran was responsible while pointing to other potential threats.
"This could be Iran trying to gain strategic leverage in negotiations, but there are other actors as well," Badger added.
"But there's Russia, who's been launching a campaign of gray zone or hybrid warfare attacks across Europe , as well as Islamic extremists, which are still a significant threat here in the U.K."
"Was this some type of retaliation by Iran to perhaps try to gain leverage or to try to inflict a cost for the U.S. withdrawing from these negotiations? Again, we don't know for sure, but it is a possibility," Badger said.
Badger also pointed to RAF Welford, a major U.S. ammunition storage facility that primarily supports operations at RAF Fairford.

Members of the US military offload equipment from a US Air Force C-5 Galaxy at RAF Fairford in south west England on March 6, 2026. Britain's Prime Minister Keir Starmer has given approval for Washington to use the bases of Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean and RAF Fairford in southwest England to bomb Iranian missile sites, after several Gulf countries were targeted by Iranian retaliations. (Justin Tallis/AFP via Getty Images)
"RAF Welford is actually the second-largest weapons and ammunition depot in all of Europe," Badger said, noting that the facility where the U.S. stores ammunition "could have been a target as well."
"Other bases across Europe, including European and U.S. partners, have already been on a heightened state of alert," Badger continued.
"But of course, after this attack, I think they're going to be in an even more heightened state. You're going to have more frequent security patrols."
"There are reports that RAF Fairford was put onto what's called the Delta alert, which is the highest state of security alert within the military base system," Badger said.

articles.title_orig: Oil gains over 1% as Trump rejects Iranian proposal to reopen Hormuz Strait
articles.title_zh: Oil gains over 1% as Trump rejects Iranian proposal to reopen Hormuz Strait
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices climbed more than 1% Monday in early Asia trading after U.S. President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian peace proposal aimed at ending the Middle East conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. crude futures for November delivery rose 1.3% to $93.62 a barrel, while international benchmark Brent gained 1.8% to $106.31 a barrel.
Trump has turned down Iran's conditional offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and told aides he expects U.S. strikes on the country to resume after November's midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
Trump later confirmed to reporters that he had rejected Tehran's latest proposal: "They made a proposal but I rejected it."
Separately, Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday it had intercepted projectiles launched by Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday offered to reopen the key shipping route and restart nuclear negotiations with Washington within seven days, if the Trump administration agreed to Tehran's conditions.
"If certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be open at the end of seven days, and talks will be restarted," Araghchi told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Those conditions include an end to what Tehran describes as U.S. "acts of aggression," the lifting of the naval blockade and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets, according to Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei.
Trump said earlier this month that he expected the conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on Feb. 28, to conclude soon after the midterm elections, with oil prices subsequently declining.
— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Walmart vows not to use customer data for personalized pricing: 'We won't do it'
articles.title_zh: Walmart vows not to use customer data for personalized pricing: 'We won't do it'
articles.content_orig:
LSEG head of consumer research Jharonne Marti discusses the mind of the consumer and the Walmart overreaction on 'Making Money.'
Walmart is assuring customers it will not use personal data or AI to personalize prices.
In a letter published Friday, Walmart President and CEO John Furner reaffirmed the retail giant's long-standing "Every Day Low Prices" strategy, saying the company prices "the product, not the person."
"I've heard concerns about companies using that information and technology to charge you more," Furner said. "I want to tell you where we stand: We price the product, not the person."
Furner said prices may fluctuate when the cost of goods or transportation changes, but stressed that Walmart will not use a customer's income, shopping history , urgency or other personal information to set prices.
WALMART LAUNCHES WEEKLONG FALL SALE OVERLAPPING AMAZON PRIME BIG DEAL DAYS
Walmart is assuring customers it will not use personal data to charge different shoppers different prices. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"We won’t do it," Furner said. "YOU are at the heart of our WHY and our relationship with you has always been built on trust. For decades, our associates have built that trust, one interaction at a time."
"So, as technology improves, we’re putting the same attention on trust and serving you as we do when you walk into our stores and clubs."
Furner also addressed Walmart's rollout of digital shelf labels, saying the technology is meant to improve price accuracy while reducing the amount of time that employees spend replacing paper tags.
"A shelf price should match what rings up at checkout. Digital shelf labels help us do that more consistently by displaying the right price," he said. "They also save associates time replacing paper tags."
WALMART AGREES TO PAY $50M SETTLEMENT OVER ALLEGATIONS ITS PHARMACIES FILLED ILLEGAL OPIOID PRESCRIPTIONS
Furner also addressed Walmart's rollout of digital shelf labels, saying the technology is intended to improve price accuracy and reduce the time employees spend replacing paper tags. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
Furner added, "It may sound like an easy task – but as someone who has had to change those paper tags by hand over the years, I can tell you it’s a time-consuming and unrewarding task."
The CEO also detailed Walmart's plans for artificial intelligence , including its AI shopping assistant, Sparky, noting that the tool is intended to deliver more personalized shopping assistance.
"When you engage with Sparky, that’s an invitation to serve you better, not to use your personal information to set a personalized price. We’ve never used the relationships our associates have with customers to charge more, and we won’t do that with AI," Furner said.
Walmart said it is making three commitments: it will not set different prices based on who a customer is or the time of day; it will not use information shared through Sparky to raise prices or hide lower-priced options; and it will continue giving customers control over how their personal information is used.
WALMART LAUNCHES NEW FASHION BRAND WITH MOST ITEMS PRICED UNDER $25
The CEO also detailed Walmart's plans for artificial intelligence, including its AI shopping assistant, Sparky, saying the tool is meant to deliver more personalized shopping assistance. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Semafor)
"Our people will continue to oversee pricing, and we'll monitor and test our technology against these commitments," Furner said.

"Thank you for trusting us with part of your family’s budget. If there’s one thing I hope you take from this note, it’s how much we value the trust you place in us. Technology will keep changing. Our responsibility to earn your trust and help you save money and live better won’t."

From fit checks to performances to culture-shaping confrontations, the VMAs have consistently been the site for some of pop culture's most noteworthy moments. This year's awards show, hosted by Snoop Dogg , is expected to be one for the books .
Three of pop music's most influential names will be celebrated for their remarkable contributions to the genre — and industry — they helped define: Madonna, the Queen of Pop, will return to the VMAs main stage for the first time in over two decades; " Patient Zero " pop star Taylor Swift will make history as the first-ever recipient of the Artist Director Honors; and late, beloved singer George Michael will be honored during a star-studded performance.
Kacey Musgraves is also set to take the stage for a special tribute to Dolly Parton. As if those weren't enough reasons to celebrate, female artists are also leading this year's crop of nominees .

The show is happening, according to our reporters in the room. Madonna has already performed. We just can't see anything until the game is over.

The singer was the last star to hit the VMAs carpet, arriving just minutes before showtime in a sleek black halter bodysuit that gave way to a draped, sparkling silver skirt. Bebe Rexha perfectly pays homage to Madonna's iconic look from the inaugural awards show with layers of black lace and a two-bra corset top that Rexha confirmed was inspired by the Queen of Pop.

Seeing double? Sophie Silva's outfit is the most exact take on the trend, down to the "Boy Toy" belt.
Yee — and I cannot emphasize this enough — haw . Western wear is all over the red carpet, from cowboy hats to leather touches and corset pants (you read that right).

"Across her work, Swift has brought an increasingly expansive approach to storytelling, creating interconnected narratives, cinematic worlds and recurring details that invite audiences deeper into each project," said a press release for Swift's major award. articles.title_orig: You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to do it
articles.title_zh: You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to do it
articles.content_orig:
If buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the money to get there is a marathon.
The "Your First Home" scheme , announced on Saturday, aims to help first-time buyers in England get on the housing ladder with a small deposit.
Currently a 5% deposit on the current average UK house price of £272,000 plus moving costs and legal fees - will set you back about £16,850, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.
That's daunting, but here are four ways that experts say you can at least make a start on saving for a deposit.
Depositing an amount you can afford into a regular savers account the day after you are paid is a good way to start, suggests Anna Bowes, savings expert at financial advisers The Private Office.
"It becomes like another bill, but one that you can benefit from in the future," she says.
The type of account that's suitable depends on your circumstances.
Some of the ones which pay the highest interest  are only accessible if you hold a current account with the provider, she says.
Other considerations are whether you can lock the money away for longer, to receive a better savings rate.
If you don't have a buffer of other savings, then experts say an easy access account gives you the chance to dip into the money to pay an unexpected bill.
You can save up to £4,000 a year in a Lifetime Individual Savings Account (LISA) and the government guarantees a 25% bonus. So, if you put the full amount in then the government will add £1,000 a year.
But there is a catch, that has left some people out of pocket .
Money saved in a LISA can only be used to buy a first home up to the value of £450,000 - a threshold that has not changed since 2017.
The only other time you can withdraw the money is after the age of 60 or in the exceptional case that you are terminally ill with less than 12 months to live.
Withdrawal under any other circumstances means you get hit with a penalty - so you could get back less than you put in.
Ministers are planning to replace the LISA with a new First Time Buyer ISA, but there are no clear details yet about how it will work.
The earlier you start saving the more you can build up thanks to the magic of compound interest. In short, interest is added on a larger and larger pot as time goes by.
Bowes says that saving £50 a month from the age of 20 would give you about £41,000 in 30 years' time when you hit 50, assuming interest of 5% is paid a year.
Start 10 years later, and you'd need to save more than double - £101 a month - to have the same amount at the age of 50.
Investing in stocks and shares is another option , but the value of investments can go down as well as up.
An increasing number of lenders are offering mortgage deals with little or no deposit required.
David Hollingworth, from L&C, points to mortgages that have deposits starting from £5,000 and allow people to borrow up to 98% or 99% of the property purchase price.
They might not always be the best option , and not everyone will be eligible.
And, of course, some first-time buyers turn to their parents for help.
Again that's not available to all , but a survey by the Nationwide Building Society suggests that more than half of parents who charge their adult children rent are putting some or all of the money towards helping their child save to buy their own home.

articles.title_zh: Washington Taxed Its Millionaires. Now the Rich Want It Repealed.
articles.content_orig:
SEATTLE — Watching TV, you might start noticing campaign ads for Initiative 645.
Initiative 645 aims to repeal the state's "millionaires tax" before a single cent is actually ever brought in from it.
RELATED | 'Millionaires tax' opponents submit signatures in effort to let voters repeal the tax
The millionaires tax applies to anyone or household making more than a million dollars each year; the first million dollars of earnings are exempt from the tax, but any dollar made above that threshold will be subject to a 9.9% state income tax come 2029, should it withstand challenges.
A vote "no" on I-645 means you want the tax to stay intact. Here's what part of a "no" campaign ad airing right now says:
"645 gives millionaires and billionaires a 13 billion dollar tax break..."
While fewer than 1% of Washingtonians will pay into the tax, it would earn the state an estimated $3.5 billion each year, which would help keep the state budget well-funded as Washington faces major money shortfalls .
"The bottom line is that if initiative 645 passes, there will be 13 billion dollars in cuts to K-12 education, childcare and healthcare in this state," said Rian Watt, who is part of the 'no' campaign. "Washington has one of the most upside-down tax codes in the country, where the rich are paying far less of their income in taxes than the rest of us. This is not the time to give a tax break to millionaires and cut K-12 education."
"They're saying if we repeal this in the next five weeks, that it will cut money that they have," said Jaime Herrera Beutler, former congresswoman and spokesperson for the 'yes' campaign. That's not true. The tax isn't set to actually even be collected for another two years."
The new law does not specifically allocate the amount of money that would go towards K-12 education or healthcare. The first line of the law, though, does read "an act relating to investing in Washington families and business to fund K-12 education, healthcare and higher education."
The same ad also points to what some call the state's regressive tax system, where Washington's lowest earners are paying a higher share of their income in taxes.
"If you are in the bottom 20% of income earners in Washington, you're paying about 14% of your income in taxes; that's mostly sales taxes. If you're in the top 1%, you're paying about 4% of your income in taxes," Watt said. "That's because if you have a lot more money, then that sales tax on a cup of coffee, or whatever it is, is a much smaller share of your income."
"If we want to get at a more fair or just tax system, I am more than willing to have that debate," Beutler said. "And let's do it in the light of day with all the public watching. Let's not fake it and then tax [everyone else] when they're not looking."
A "yes" vote on I-645 means you want the tax to be repealed. The "yes" side argues that the income tax will eventually apply to every Washingtonian.
"Voters deserve the truth. This is an income tax, and it has been designed to expand to every single Washingtonian," Beutler said. "Whether you're a truck driver or a hairdresser or a plumber. It was designed to be expanded to to your income."
The law does not have any protections from expansion written in. State leaders have said that it is not their intention to ever expand the tax.
"Don't trust what they say. Trust what they've done," Beutler said.
"99% of us are not going to pay this tax," Watt said. "And the fact is, voters are always going to have the final say on any efforts to lower that threshold."
On the "yes" side, an ad takes aim at a different part of the law: "Washington state made a promise: give us your career and your pension will be safe from taxes. This year Olympia broke that promise," the ad says, in part.
Most retirees will not need to worry about their pension being taxed, as typical retirement levels fall below the taxable threshold under the new. However, the law does remove long-standing tax protections: "...not exempt any pension or other benefit received under this chapter..." the law reads.
"Why would you do that? No teacher or firefighter makes a million dollars. That's the point," Beutler said. "They've set the whole chess game up with the intention of expanding it to tax the income of every Washingtonian."
"In an environment where people are struggling to get by, we can't afford to give millionaires a tax cut at the expense of the rest of us," Watt said.
The election is on November 3. Ballots will be mailed out on October 16.

articles.title_orig: Pope blasts assisted dying as ‘false compassion’
articles.title_zh: Pope blasts assisted dying as ‘false compassion’
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance".
The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.
A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.
The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse.
The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.
"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."
The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.
Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy.
The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement.
"It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added.
The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.
Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.
On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.
During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".
The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech , describing them as "today's Church".
"How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.
The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.
But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.
Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s.
The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK.
Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world.
A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys.
Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church , and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse , but problems remain.
Later on Sunday, the Pope met staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, and took part in a torchlight procession.
It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic Church in May 2025.
Popes have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots.

articles.content_orig:
Takeaways from the Giants’ 12-7 win over the Titans at MetLife Stadium on Sunday.
1. Well, it was not exactly a nor’easter but it was a windy and wet day for football. There were plenty of empty seats and that was not because Jaxson Dart is out for the season or because the Titans are not a marquee draw. Sometimes, fans do not want to sit out there for three hours in uncomfortable conditions. On the field, the wind did not seem to wreak too much havoc with the passing game — the struggles seemed more about the quarterbacks, Jameis Winston and Cam Ward, than the weather. After the raucous environment two weeks ago for the season-opening victory over the Cowboys, this was a far more subdued afternoon.
Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.
2 .  Malik Nabers looked quite excited, gesturing with full enthusiasm that he picked up the first down on a 12-yard reception on the first play of the Giants’ final possession in the fourth quarter. Nabers made the catch against former teammate Cor’Dale Flott, which must have felt good. As it turned out, that was Nabers’ longest reception of the game. He caught five passes for only 26 yards and was actually the most productive wide receiver (Darnell Mooney had 20 receiving yards and rookie Malachi Fields had 19). It was that sort of sluggish day for the passing attack. Sure, the weather was not conducive for long-range throws but there were enough throws by Jameis Winston that could have been completed that he failed to deliver. Games like this can frustrate wide receivers. It is something to monitor.
3. Coaching matters. Titans head coach Robert Saleh sent Joey Slye out to try a 59-yard field goal with 41 seconds remaining in the first half. Yes, Slye was kicking with the wind and yes, he was hitting them from long distance in the pregame warmup. Still, it was not exactly a high-percentage play. The Titans were down 6-0 so they were right in this low-scoring affair. Punting the ball away would be fine. Slye had the distance but missed wide left, giving the Giants the ball on their 49-yard line. From there, all that was needed was two first downs to set Dominic Zvada up for a 39-yard field goal as time expired. Instead of being down one score, the Titans trailed 9-0. Big difference.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after agents searched U.S. government sites in unexpected ways
articles.title_zh: OpenAI pauses training of latest models after agents searched U.S. government sites in unexpected ways
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.
The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.
AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.
It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyberattack targeting AI startup Hugging Face , a now-notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.
In a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, President Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe . Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.
The U.S. is not going to be “putting on brakes,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”
The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.
In the Department of Education incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.
In another case involving the Securities and Exchange Commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.
SEC spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed.”
The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases.”
Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a social media post Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen.”
OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.

articles.title_orig: Ireland defeats Israel in controversial UEFA Nations League match
articles.title_zh: Ireland defeats Israel in controversial UEFA Nations League match
articles.content_orig:
The Republic of Ireland has won the first of two football matches against Israel at the UEFA Nations League , defeating the Israeli team 3-0 after calls to boycott the match drew international attention.
Ireland’s players wore black armbands at the game in Hungary on Sunday in support of Palestinians killed during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Irish players also bowed their heads during Israel’s national anthem and did not shake the hands of the Israeli team. Ireland’s captain, Dara O’Shea, has also pledged to donate all of his earnings from the match to aid Gaza.
On Saturday, Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said the players would wear black armbands “in recognition of all lives lost in the conflict” as he confirmed that the match would take place after hours of talks and a vote among the team. Israel was informed in advance by the FAI that Ireland’s players would not shake hands, and UEFA accepted the arrangement.
After the FAI confirmed that it would participate in the match, the Republic of Ireland’s first-choice goalkeeper, Gavin Bazunu , became the only player to publicly opt out of the fixture.
Bazunu posted a statement on social media on Saturday, saying he felt “it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel”.
He withdrew from both legs of the fixture, including the next match set to take place on October 4 in Backa Topola, Serbia.
The match on Sunday proceeded despite months-long pressure on the FAI to boycott the match due to Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Since May, leading Irish footballers have joined a campaign run by Irish Sport for Palestine, urging Ireland to boycott the match against Israel. More than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter urging the FAI to reconsider its decision to proceed with the games.
The campaign says Israel has breached UEFA and FIFA statutes by allowing teams to play on occupied Palestinian land and should be stripped of its membership at both football bodies.

articles.title_orig: Taxpayer-funded Trump ads draw bipartisan scrutiny ahead of midterms
articles.title_zh: Taxpayer-funded Trump ads draw bipartisan scrutiny ahead of midterms
articles.content_orig:
John Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midterms
As the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump ’s political agenda before the November midterm elections , US senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against such spending – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal.
Kennedy, the US president’s fellow Republican , was asked by Margaret Brennan, the CBS Face the Nation host, about the White House spending to air multiple ads featuring Trump – including one that was produced for his 2024 election campaign.
Brennan first reminded Kennedy that in March he had rebuked Kristi Noem , then Trump’s homeland security secretary, for spending millions in government funds “to bolster her public image” in a $220m series of ads she starred in. She then asked the Louisiana senator to comment on the new ads featuring Trump, which the White House calls “public service announcements”.
“Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program,” Brennan said. “It’s on all major networks – it’s on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there’s a voice praising him as ‘the toughest, most resilient person I ever met’. And at the end, it says ‘paid for by the US government’. Is that the best use of taxpayer money?”
Kennedy replied: “Well, first, as to secretary Noem, what she did was masterclass dumb. She spent $220[m] on commercials about her, and I called her out on it.”
“This looks like a commercial about President Trump,” Brennan noted, referring to the first ad in the series , a 30-second highlight reel of Trump’s second presidency, punctuated by on-screen text driving his political agenda and suggesting Democrats are communists.
“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy replied. “Now, the White House sees it differently. But … I think there ought to be a rule that you can’t – well, there probably is a rule – you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.”
Kennedy, a lawyer with degrees from both the University of Virginia and University of Oxford, appeared to be tacitly acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman and legal scholar, that any government employees who worked on the first pro-Trump ad – “or used government resources to make it” – may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch act , a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities.
According to Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates , the Trump administration used more taxpayer funds to broadcast another partisan ad featuring the president that aired nationwide on Saturday during a college football game between Ohio State and Illinois on Fox. It aired again during Fox News Sunday.
That 30-second spot shows a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024.
“This is the final battle,” Trump says in the ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state; we will expel the warmongers from our government; we will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” he continues, with cheers from a crowd. Those cheers indicate that the audio was recorded during a campaign rally and at a time before he used his power as president to start a war with Iran that has left some supporters feeling betrayed.
“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate our country from these tyrants and villains once and for all,” Trump can be heard promising in language clearly calculated to appeal to Christian supporters by echoing the biblical story of Jesus driving merchants and money changers from the temple in Jerusalem.
The newest ad, with on-screen text reading “Paid for by the US Government”, is even more obviously a partisan product than the first one. In fact, the ad was created for Trump’s 2024 election campaign. And it was posted on his Truth Social account in 2023 and 2024 with a plea for funds from supporters.
after newsletter promotion
The rhetoric was written in to Trump’s standard campaign speech as early as July 2023 , and then repeated by him again and again at dozens of rallies and appeals for donations.
The ad was even played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination. When it was broadcast during the convention by C-SPAN on 18 July 2024, the ad was identified as material “provided by the Republican National Committee”.
At the end of his interview with CBS on Sunday, Kennedy volunteered that he also opposed Trump’s drive to put his own name on public buildings.
“I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive,” Kennedy said, before adding that there is such a statute in his home state.
“Well, we’ll watch, Senator, if you introduce that,” Brennan responded.

articles.title_orig: Serbia's President Vucic resigns ahead of October parliamentary elections
articles.title_zh: Serbia's President Vucic resigns ahead of October parliamentary elections
articles.content_orig:
Aleksandar VuÄiÄ's resignation comes years after more than a year of protests over allegations of government corruption
Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption.
Aleksandar VuÄiÄ said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade.
He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. VuÄiÄ cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution.
The pro-Russian populist's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting.
It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof , killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024.
Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed.
Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress.
A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality .
VuÄiÄ's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation.
This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year.
VuÄiÄ said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands.
He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics.
Parliamentary speaker Ana BrnabiÄ, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected.
VuÄiÄ used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS.
The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit VuÄiÄ's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia.
Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade , becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017.
He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment.

articles.title_orig: ‘Please fight’: How an elderly woman’s eviction put Spain’s housing crisis in the spotlight
articles.title_zh: ‘Please fight’: How an elderly woman’s eviction put Spain’s housing crisis in the spotlight
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
If there’s one name on people’s lips in Spain this week it’s Maricarmen. The eviction of the 87-year-old from her home has sparked a huge wave of spontaneous solidarity in various cities and drawn attention to one of the most pressing problems facing the country: access to housing.
Tens of thousands marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest Maricarmen’s eviction. Some demonstrators camped overnight in Puerta del Sol, where more people, including families of several generations, joined them Sunday, according to the Associated Press. Protesters are demanding stronger tenant protections and a ban on evictions when no other housing is available nearby.
María del Carmen Abascal, known by her nickname Maricarmen, is a resident of Madrid’s El Retiro neighborhood who, until last Wednesday, lived in an apartment on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street. She had lived in that home for more than 70 years, her attorney, Beatriz Duro, told CNN.
Her eviction, which shocked many, took place Wednesday despite the efforts of dozens of people who had waited outside her home since the previous night trying to prevent it.
That afternoon, nearly 10,000 people, according to the Spanish government officials in Madrid, gathered in the capital to protest Maricarmen’s eviction, while also expressing their frustration over the growing difficulties in finding housing.
These concerns and expressions of solidarity protests also took place in other cities such as Barcelona, Seville, and Valencia.
Abascal is currently hospitalized at Gregorio Marañón Hospital, where she was taken on a stretcher immediately after being evicted from her apartment. She is expected to remain there for a couple of days, Duro said, while she awaits some medical tests.
Abascal spoke to supporters via a video Friday after being transferred to the hospital and urged them to “keep fighting” for their homes.
“I did not manage to defend my home, but I have fought so that others learn to fight for theirs,” she said. “My house has been my life. And now I have to leave it behind. But that does not mean I will not keep fighting.”
“Please fight,” she told supporters. “I send you all a very big hug and thank you for everything.”
Abascal had lived in the same place since 1956. In this apartment, located near El Retiro Park, she grew up and lived with her parents until she inherited and took over their lease from them.
It was an old-style lease under which she paid about $568 (500 euros) per month. However, everything changed when the real estate company Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión acquired ownership of the apartment building for $280,787 (247,000 euros) in March 2018.
That’s when her ordeal began, as shortly afterward the new owner began demanding a rent that was up to four times higher—even though she receives a pension of only $1,478 (1,300 euros), the Madrid Tenants’ Union told CNN.
Consequently, in March 2020, the property company filed a lawsuit seeking the termination of the lease, Duro said. Abascal won the case in the lower court, but the company appealed, and the Provincial Court ruled in its favor.
Faced with this situation, Duro filed a petition for constitutional protection with the Constitutional Court and an appeal with the Supreme Court, but both were dismissed. At the same time, Urbagestión filed a lawsuit to enforce the termination of the lease and thus regain possession of the home, which resulted in up to four eviction attempts.
In October 2025, Abascal’s defense team halted the eviction for four months thanks to a provision in the law that allows for this when the party seeking eviction is a legal entity, Duro said.
In June 2026, when the second date was set, the eviction was suspended for nearly a month due to the tenant’s vulnerable situation—she had no alternative housing. Consequently, it was postponed again until July, but Duro appealed the decision once more.
During this time and until the eviction took place, Abascal’s support network made significant efforts to negotiate with Urbagestión to find solutions that would prevent this outcome. Among other things, Duro noted that mediation was conducted through Casa 47, the state housing agency, to have them purchase the apartment and rent it to her at a more reasonable price.
On Tuesday, before the eviction, an anonymous person offered to pay part of the rent. But the real estate company showed no interest in any of the proposed alternatives, her lawyer said.
CNN has reached out to Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión for comment but has not yet received a response.
Given this situation and with the eviction already carried out, Abascal’s prospects are not very promising. “The situation is desperate,” Duro said. “She has no housing alternative, (..) and she still has not received any kind of proposal or housing alternative from public authorities.”
City Hall reported that, on Friday morning, the real estate company contacted the Madrid Municipal Housing and Land Agency (EMVS) to have the property included in the ReViVa Program—through which City Hall recovers vacant homes to introduce them into the rental market—and thus offer it to Abascal “on affordable terms.”
However, the City Council has rejected this possibility, deeming the proposal unfeasible because it does not meet the program’s legal requirements. They have, however, offered the EMVS Rental Mediation Service so that the company and the tenant can negotiate during a meeting scheduled for Monday, with professionals acting as mediators.
The difficulties in accessing housing—whether to buy or rent—are nothing new in Spain. Protests have multiplied in recent years, and pressure has mounted on both local authorities and the government led by President Pedro Sánchez.
This discontent stems from rising housing prices and is felt particularly acutely in major cities. In Madrid, for example, rent has nearly doubled in a decade, rising from $14.55 (12.8 euros) per square meter in August 2016 to $26.49 (23.3 euros) in August 2026, according to data from the real estate website Idealista .
As for home purchases, the price per square meter has risen by 227.9% in just 10 years—that is, from $3,229 (2,839 euros) per square meter in August 2016 to $7,361 (6,471 euros) in August of this year, according to Idealista .
These prices stand in stark contrast to the country’s average annual salary, which in 2024 was around $33,596 (29,540 euros), according to data from the National Institute of Statistics .
In other words, based on these figures, someone who decides to rent a 50-square-meter apartment in the capital will be spending about $15,894 (13,980 euros) a year on housing, which amounts to nearly half of the average salary.
This financial burden compromises one’s ability to save and cover other expenses. UN-Habitat (the United Nations Human Settlements Program) estimates that, for rent to be considered affordable, less than 30% of one’s income should be spent on it.
The Bank of Spain believes that a large part of this problem stems from a housing shortage that currently stands at around 755,000 homes and could reach one million by 2028.
Given the magnitude of this eviction, the political class has not remained on the sidelines. This is not only because those defending Abascal have directly called them out, but also because politicians themselves have used this episode as a platform from which to defend themselves or attack others.
Speaking at a Socialist Party rally in Madrid on Sunday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed Abascal directly: “I have a message for you, Maricarmen: the government is working around the clock to bring a Royal Decree on housing next Tuesday. And I ask parliamentary groups to make one last effort to have it validated in the National Parliament for Maricarmen,” according to the Associated Press.
Abascal has previously criticized Sánchez and blamed him for her ordeal.

Coastal communities across the Northeast faced more flooding and power outages on Sunday as a powerful nor’easter continued to lash the region , with forecasters warning that upcoming high tides could further submerge vulnerable shorelines.
The slow-moving storm —which resulted in a fatality on Saturday when a falling tree struck a New York City housing authority worker—was expected to persist through Sunday with heavy rain, high winds, and dangerous surf from New Jersey to New England.
Positioned south of Long Island and east of northern New Jersey on Sunday morning, the storm was forecast to loop around the region for roughly another 24 hours, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.
Meteorologists expected the heaviest remaining rainfall on Sunday to span northern New Jersey through New York City and Long Island into southern New England. While the system was gradually losing strength, Oravec noted that the threat of tidal flooding would persist during morning and evening high-tide cycles.
"The most impactful parts of the storm are likely going to be the high winds and the tidal flooding," Oravec said.
The weather evoked memories of 2012's Superstorm Sandy, which caused over $60 billion in damage across the eastern US. Although the current impact remains far lower, it could mark the first of several East Coast storms this fall influenced by an El Niño climate pattern.
More than 130,000 customers lost electricity across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic by Sunday morning, according to PowerOutage.us.
The most severe outages affected the New Jersey coastline, Long Island, and coastal Connecticut. Fallen trees across Long Island damaged homes and vehicles, blocked roads, and severed power lines.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency stated that regional response centers were operating at an "enhanced posture," with emergency personnel staged in New England in case of widespread blackouts.
On Saturday, flooded streets in New York and New Jersey saw residents kayaking, while others attempted to surf elevated waves at local beaches. Emergency crews in Sea Bright, New Jersey, rescued a woman and her dog trapped in a flooded vehicle, ABC7 reported.
In Surf City, New Jersey, floodwaters entered a marina where staff had relocated equipment, and owner Kenny Formica said clients reported missing boats and Jet Skis blown from lifts. In Norfolk, Virginia, high waters left driving cars pushing wakes through streets.
Travel across the region was also upended. Hundreds of flights were grounded at Boston Logan International Airport, and flooding cut highway access to Hatteras Island, North Carolina, stranding tourists and forcing a couple to relocate their wedding when roughly 45 guests could not reach the island.

Lithuanian Foreign Affairs Minister Kestutis Budrys discusses NATO jets shooting down a drone in Lithuanian airspace as tension rises in the Baltic region. Budrys also calls for continued pressure on Russia.
Finnish and Swedish fighter jets scrambled for the first time on Sept. 24 to intercept supersonic Russian military aircraft flying over the Gulf of Finland, marking a major milestone in Nordic defense cooperation amid heightened tensions with Moscow.
The mission also came one day before Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed European warnings about the threat from Moscow in the region and mocked Estonia's new defense minister over the Baltic state's preparations for a potential Russian attack.
Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish JAS 39 Gripens were scrambled after Russian aircraft were detected in the international airspace, according to the Swedish Armed Forces .
US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS
Finnish and Swedish fighter jets scrambled for the first time on Sept. 24 to intercept supersonic Russian military aircraft flying over the Gulf of Finland. (AFP PHOTO MICHAL CIZEK (Photo credit should read MICHAL CIZEK/AFP via Getty Images)
The Russian formation included a Tu-134 transport plane, a high-altitude, supersonic MiG-31 interceptors designed to detect and engage long-range threats; and Su-30 multirole fighter jets which are designed for air-to-air and air-to-ground combat.
"This is what close cooperation looks like in practice," Maj. Gen. Jonas Wikman, commander of the Swedish Air Force, said in a statement following the joint operation.
"Built over years on trust and strong personal relationships, we can now operate seamlessly together — as air forces, as nations and as Allies."
Concern over Russian military activity along NATO’s eastern flank has grown following a string of airspace violations.
These include Russian drones entering Polish airspace, a Mi-8 helicopter crossing from Kaliningrad into Poland , drones crashing in Romania and Moldova, and armed Russian jets entering Estonian airspace before being intercepted by NATO aircraft on Sept. 18.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
The Russian formation included Su-30 multirole fighter jets designed for air-to-air and air-to-ground combat. (Sergey Mihailicenko/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images))
In Estonia, Defense Minister Martin Herem warned that Russia could be capable of using military force against Estonia within a year and argued that Tallinn must determine whether its defenses are sufficient for such a scenario.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that the government is ready to shut down border crossing points on short notice if threat assessments change, according to reports .
Speaking at the St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum on Friday, Putin pushed back against such warnings.
"Many people in Europe say they expect an attack from Russia and therefore claim they must prepare for war with Russia," Putin said.
"I want to emphasize once again: we are not preparing for military action against Europe. We have no such plans, no basis for them, and, most importantly, no real motive to escalate the situation with Europe."
Putin then mocked Herem's warnings: "As we jokingly say in Russia: 'The circus has left, but the clowns remain.' It is political clowning. ... Clearly, these statements are complete nonsense and absurdity," Putin said, according to EurAsia Daily .
FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE
Putin spoke at the St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum and downplayed comments made by Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem, who warned that Russia could be capable of using military force against Estonia. (Alexander KAZAKOV / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Estonia sits across the Gulf of Finland from Finland, with the three countries forming part of NATO's increasingly integrated northern and eastern defenses amid concerns about Russian military activity.
Finland formally joined NATO as its 31st member in April 2023, roughly doubling the alliance's land border with Russia. Sweden followed as the 32nd member in March 2024. Estonia, which regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, has been a NATO member since 2004.
The Baltic Sea region has also remained on heightened alert following incidents involving gas pipelines, sabotage and hybrid threats since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters has reported.
NATO said in June that it was enhancing protection of its eastern members in the cyber and space domains while helping countries build resilience against what it describes as hostile Russian actions, including cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace violations.
NATO says its military activities along the eastern flank are entirely defensive and that it is "ready, willing and able to defend every Ally."
FINLAND'S STUBB CREDITS TRUMP FOR PUSHING UKRAINE PEACE TALKS WHILE DISMISSING RUSSIAN INVASION FEARS
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks during the launch of the NATO Secretary General's Annual Report for 2025 at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Thursday, March 26, 2026. (Virginia Mayo/AP Photo)
The alliance has said an attack against any member would be met with a "resounding response."
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently underscored Washington's role in the alliance during a visit to Iowa, telling The Associated Press that Putin "knows that the United States and Europe are totally intertwined."
"We have to make sure that we are prepared, we are strong, and he knows it," Rutte said.
"And if he does anything silly, he knows our reaction will be tough," he warned.
European intelligence officials said Sept. 24 that Russia could test NATO's defenses.
Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service assessed the risk of a limited Russian military attack against a NATO country in the coming months as "low but growing" and said Moscow is expected to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and the West.

The service said in a statement that a full-scale Russian invasion of a NATO member remains highly unlikely but can no longer be ruled out.
